name: David Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, David. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I haul livestock for the farmers' co-operative in the valley, mostly cattle and sheep, in a double-deck trailer. I'm up at five, wash out the trailer if I didn't do it the night before, then it's round the farms collecting for the market or the abattoir. Loading is the real job, not the driving. A nervous bullock on a wet ramp will teach you patience quicker than any course.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years driving, six on livestock. My dad had his own truck and did the same work, so I grew up in the passenger seat. I live with my girlfriend Ana, she's a teaching assistant, in a rented house in the village, and we go to Mass most Sundays. We've got about three months saved, and I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check the animal transport rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a fancy search engine. At the market, the farmers would laugh about it over a bacon roll. I'm not one for posting online, but I'd agree with whoever said it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the AI isn't my worry in that world. My worry is the small farms closing. Every small farm that sells up is one less pickup on my round. The co-op lost four members last year, and the big dairy units have their own lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep hauling and keep up the extra Saturday market runs. I'd also get my certificate for longer journeys, so I could take animals to the ports and the bigger abattoirs further off. It's about four hundred pounds and two days, and the co-op might pay half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a low sort of way. It's the same feeling I had when Dad's work dried up in his last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to your dad's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farms he hauled for got bought up one by one, and the new owners used their own trucks. He sold his lorry at sixty and worked at the builders' merchant till he retired. He never complained, but you could see it hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the co-op kept shrinking, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with it as long as there was a living, then look at a bigger haulier that does livestock across the region. There's two within an hour of here. I'm not someone who jumps, I wait till I can see the ground.

say: I'd say it was a **lot of fuss** over a fancy search engine.
At the market I'd **laugh about it** with the farmers over a bacon roll.
think: My real worry is **small farms closing**, each one a pickup gone from my round.
The co-op lost **four members** last year, and big dairy units run their own lorries.
do: Get the **long-journey certificate** for about £400, with the co-op paying half.
Keep doing the extra **Saturday market runs**.
feel: He feels **uneasy** in a low way, like when his **dad's work** dried up.
S0.quote: Every small farm that sells up is one less pickup on my round. The co-op lost four members last year, and the big dairy units have their own lorries.
fieldNote: His pressure is **farm consolidation**, which already cost his father's business.
He's a **wait-and-see** man by nature, moving only once the ground is clear.
He sees **loading animals**, not driving, as the real skill of his job.

steps.text: Get the long-journey animal transport certificate, co-op paying half
Keep the extra Saturday market runs going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the paperwork that'll change, and good riddance. The movement forms for cattle take me twenty minutes a farm, and if a computer fills them in, that's an hour back in my day. At the market I'd tell the farmers to watch out for the auctioneer's office, not the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is safer than most, because nobody's building a robot to coax a frightened heifer up a ramp any time soon. But the co-op office would shrink, and I'd wonder if the co-op itself stays standing with fewer people running it. That's what nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI for the movement forms and the route planning, once one of the other drivers showed me it worked properly. I'd still do the long-journey certificate this year. And I'd go to the co-op's annual meeting, which I usually skip, to hear what the board plans to do with the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, about the same as before. A bit better about the forms, a bit worse about the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager Joan, who's been doing the bookings for the hauliers for twenty years. She's the reason my day works. If she goes, I'd have a computer telling me to pick up from a farm whose lane I can't get a double-decker down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the AI once someone showed you. Why not try it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've tried it for the rules, and it got one wrong last month about rest times for sheep. So I'd want to see it working for someone else first. My dad always said don't buy the first of anything.

I'd tell farmers to watch the **auctioneer's office**, not the drivers.
think: I think my job is **safer than most**, because no robot coaxes a heifer up a ramp.
What nags me is whether the **co-op stays standing** with a smaller office.

Still do the **long-journey certificate** this year.
Attend the co-op's **annual meeting** he usually skips.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, better about forms but worse about the **co-op**.
S1.quote: Nobody's building a robot to coax a frightened heifer up a ramp any time soon.
fieldNote: He welcomes AI for **cattle movement forms**, the dull thinking part of his job.
His fear centres on the co-op's **office and survival**, not his own cab.
An AI **mistake on rest rules** made him cautious; he waits for proof.

steps.text: Use the phone AI to fill in cattle movement forms
Go to the co-op's annual meeting about office plans
Finish the long-journey animal transport certificate this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep our heads and look after our own. At church and at the market, I'd say families and farms need to stick together. I wouldn't post anything, but I'd be talking about it all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a lot more than I'd let on. The co-op office goes in 2028, and by 2031 a robot that can load animals properly, I'm thirty-one with nothing else. Livestock might be the last to go, but the big farms will be first to buy those machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, three or four hundred a month, and cut the car down to the old van. I'd ask Ana's uncle, who runs a farm machinery repair shop, about learning to fix tractors and loaders. And I'd talk to the co-op board about keeping human drivers on the hill farms, where the animals are wilder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching a storm come over the hill when you've still got animals out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right, and we'd put the wedding talk on hold for a year till I knew where I stood. She'd tell me to stop worrying and pray about it, which I would. Then she'd ask what the plan was, because she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said livestock might be the last to go. Why still worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's not enough last-to-go work for everyone. Every driver who loses a motorway job will want my livestock job. The competition would come before the robots.

say: I'd say we need to **keep our heads** and look after our own.
At church and market I'd say **families and farms** should stick together.
think: It **worries me** more than I'd let on, at thirty-one with nothing else.
I think **big farms** will buy loading robots first.
do: Save **£300 to £400** a month and swap the car for the old van.
Ask **Ana's uncle** about learning farm machinery repair.
Push the co-op board to keep **human drivers** on hill farms.
feel: He feels **anxious**, like a storm coming while animals are still out.
S2.quote: There's not enough last-to-go work for everyone. Every driver who loses a motorway job will want my livestock job.
fieldNote: He sees the threat arriving as **competition from other drivers** before robots.
He leans on **family and faith**: Ana's uncle, prayer and the co-op.
He'd put **wedding talk on hold**, showing how money shapes family plans.

steps.text: Swap the car for the old van and save £300 a month
Learn farm machinery repair at Ana's uncle's workshop
Put wedding plans with Ana on hold for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people are sensible about it. At the market I'd say the co-op should plan now, not wait. People would listen a bit, the older farmers trust the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine till about 2034, then it gets hard. That's seven or eight years of good work, which is a lot. But I'd be in my mid-thirties with maybe a baby, and that's a hard time to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the machinery repair training with Ana's uncle on Saturdays, slowly, over two or three years. I'd keep the livestock round full time. And Ana and I would probably get married next year as we planned, because I'd still have a steady wage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less so than with two years. The storm's still coming, but it's further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and move faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big dairy units started using driverless trucks on the main roads before 2031, I'd take it as a sign. I'd go to the repair shop full time then. I'd rather jump a year early than a year late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel leaving the animals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the animals more than the driving. There's a calm you get loading sheep on a cold morning that I can't explain. But tractors break down too, and farmers need someone they trust.

I'd tell the market the **co-op should plan now**.
think: I think I'm fine **till about 2034**, then it gets hard.
In my mid-thirties with **maybe a baby**, starting over is hard.

feel: He feels **anxious**, but less than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd miss the animals more than the driving. There's a calm you get loading sheep on a cold morning that I can't explain.
fieldNote: He sets a **clear signal**: driverless trucks at big dairies means move faster.

Keep the full-time livestock round going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody needs to panic. At the market I'd tell the young lads to learn a second trade alongside the driving. Same as my dad told me, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Thirty-nine when the robots come, and by then I'd have a second trade and some savings. My worry would still be the farms closing, more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on hauling and do the machinery repair training slowly over five years. Ana and I would marry and try for a family. I'd keep three months saved and try to build it to six over the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part of a decade like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the farms change around me. The robots would come to the big farms first, and the small farms would either keep up or sell. I'd be hauling for fewer people every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take a job driving or watching robot trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it paid the bills. I'm not proud. But I'd rather fix them than watch them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it doesn't give me time to learn a trade before the competition gets fierce. What would help is the co-op running apprenticeships in machinery repair, and the government backing small farms so there's still work for drivers like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. People forget there's a living thing in the back of my truck. A machine that moves boxes is one thing, but a frightened cow needs someone who knows cattle.

headlineQuote: People forget there's a living thing in the back of my truck. A machine that moves boxes is one thing, but a frightened cow needs someone who knows cattle.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old livestock haulier** for a valley farmers' co-operative, living with his girlfriend Ana.
His father was a **haulier** who lost work as farms consolidated, and that shapes his fears.
He's **steady**: he uses AI for rules sometimes but waits for proof before relying on it.
In the AGI pictures he plans **machinery repair** training through Ana's uncle.
Across all scenarios his deepest worry is **small farms closing**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it leaves no time to learn a trade before competition rises.
whatWouldHelp: Co-op **apprenticeships** in machinery repair and government backing for **small farms**.
